doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Cable channels refusing residuals and the Annie Lennox SNL appearance
summary: Cable channels do not sign union agreements or pay residuals; Levin compares NBC with Comedy Central reruns of his Saturday Night Live work with Annie Lennox.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: It’s a kind of a one-shot.

There are a lot of cable channels, very successful ones, who don’t, they’re not signatory to anything, the musicians’ unions, actors unions, ASCAP, BMI, they just don’t sign the contracts. And all this stuff has been taken for granted over to the big networks, they all do, they just don’t do it. They realize they can get music and performances for nothing. Just don’t agree to anything and you’ve got it. Another typical example is I’ve done “Saturday Night Live” a couple of times with the guest music artist. Most recently it was with Annie Lennox a few years ago when she was doing a promo tour and we did “Saturday Night Live.”
As a member of her band.

Yeah. NBC re-ran it that summer as just part of their rerun segment, and everything was on union contract and we got paid for it, which — hey — we’re doing this for a living. That’s the concept. But Comedy Central reruns that show once a month or so and they don’t pay residuals. That’s more the norm I’m sorry to say.
How come somebody can’t do something about that?

They try. It’s not easy. It takes a big legal fight and ASCAP and BMI especially, they get to these things as they can but the whole music industry has changed so massively in the last ten, fifteen years. As technology changes the whole pattern of the way people are purchasing music changes. Right now we just saw the Napster stuff go down which was confusing just even for the people that are involved in it, and for the rest of us just watching. Was this good” Is it bad? I don’t understand. I don’t get it. And where did it come down. Even the way it came down was complicated with facing some realities. Okay they’re losing this country, but it’s just a website. They could just start the website up in France or something that doesn’t subscribe to the same copyright laws. They could just do it from there. So people are writing music and hoping to get paid for it are saying what are we doing for a living? What’s happening?
